lectures.description: Establish a working training pipeline and load your starting pretrained architecture.

sessions.title: Choosing the Development Environment
sessions.description: Compare hardware accelerators like GPUs and TPUs with CPUs, and configure accessible notebook environments (e.g., Google Colab).
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome learners to this session! Today, we are opening the engine bay of machine learning infrastructure to understand where our computations actually live. A common point of confusion for beginners is treating a machine learning model like standard software that runs efficiently on any standard processor. We will begin on the virtual whiteboard by drawing a stark contrast between a Central Processing Unit (CPU) and a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). The CPU is like a highly skilled, versatile craftsman—it handles complex sequential logic beautifully, but only operates on a few tasks at once. Conversely, a GPU is like an assembly line of thousands of simple workers; it cannot handle complex general computing tasks well, but it performs massive, simultaneous simple arithmetic. Because deep learning is fundamentally built on massive matrix multiplications, we need this parallel assembly line to train our models in hours instead of weeks.

After establishing this visual intuition, we will transition to setting up a practical cloud-based environment. Rather than forcing learners to spend hours configuring local CUDA drivers, which often leads to frustrating environment errors, we will guide them to use cloud-hosted notebook environments like Google Colab. On our virtual whiteboard, we will sketch out how a notebook interface connects to a remote virtual machine. We will walk through the critical step of checking hardware availability, showing how to execute system diagnostics such as the 'nvidia-smi' command. This command acts as our dashboard, revealing the GPU model, its memory capacity, and current utilization.

We will then address a vital diagnostic scenario: what happens when high-performance hardware accelerators are restricted or unavailable? This is a common pitfall where students get stuck when cloud quotas are exceeded. We will explain how to adapt. If forced to work on a CPU, we must adjust our training strategies by shrinking our batch sizes, utilizing smaller subset datasets for debugging, or selecting highly distilled architectures. This interactive check ensures learners understand that while a GPU is ideal for training, a CPU is perfectly adequate for sanity-checking code before launching full-scale operations.

We will conclude the session by demonstrating a diagnostic drill. We will simulate a scenario where the system diagnostic command returns an error or reveals that only a CPU is connected. The instructor will guide learners to dynamically adjust their expectations and select the appropriate fallback training options. This prepares them for real-world development where resource constraints are the norm rather than the exception.

tasks: Check hardware availability using system diagnostic tools.
Select appropriate training options when hardware resources are restricted.

sessions.title: Selecting a Pretrained Model
sessions.description: Navigate model hubs (e.g., Hugging Face) to find lightweight architectures suitable for basic text classification.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by gathering students around the virtual whiteboard to conceptualize the vast landscape of open-source model hubs, specifically Hugging Face. The goal is to demystify how we select a starting checkpoint. Start by drawing a simple taxonomy of model architectures. Explain that while there are thousands of models available, they generally fall into three major buckets: Encoder-only, Decoder-only, and Encoder-Decoder. Clarify that for our target classification task, Encoder-only models like BERT or DistilBERT are highly specialized and computationally efficient because they process text bidirectionally, generating rich dense representations of sentences without the overhead of generating new text token-by-token. This conceptual framing helps prevent the common novice mistake of downloading a massive generative model (like a 7B parameter LLM) for a straightforward classification task, saving valuable resource overhead from day one.

Transition the whiteboard visual to focus on the 'anatomy of a model name' and the trade-offs of model scale. Draw a scale showing parameter size on one side and resource requirements on the other. Use DistilBERT (approx. 66 million parameters) and BERT-base (approx. 110 million parameters) as concrete examples. Walk through how these numbers translate to physical memory (VRAM) requirements during training, introducing the rule of thumb that every billion parameters requires roughly 4 gigabytes of memory just to load the weights, and significantly more during the backward pass of training. Explain that for a resource-constrained environment like a free Google Colab instance, a lightweight model like DistilBERT is the optimal target because it retains over 95% of BERT's performance while being 40% smaller and 60% faster.

Now, simulate navigating a model card on the whiteboard. Draw a mockup of a Hugging Face repository page, pointing out the critical metadata fields that developers must check before downloading. Highlight the model size, the pipeline tag (such as 'fill-mask' or 'text-classification'), and the supported language. Address a frequent pitfall here: selecting a model trained on a completely different language domain (e.g., using an English-only model for multilingual feedback classification) or choosing an outdated architecture that lacks official integration with modern training libraries. Emphasize that checking these details early prevents downstream errors when loading the tokenizer.

Conclude with an interactive scenario-based exercise written on the whiteboard. Present the students with a hypothetical scenario: they have a dataset of customer feedback and are training on a system with a tight 16GB VRAM limit. Display three candidate models with varying parameter counts and base architectures. Guide the students to evaluate each candidate based on compatibility, memory footprint, and training speed. Through this exercise, demonstrate how to rule out oversized or structurally unsuitable candidates, reinforcing the systematic selection process and giving them the confidence to select the perfect base architecture for any resource-constrained downstream task.

tasks: Compare parameters, sizes, and compatibility of different base models.
Identify the optimal pretrained target for a resource-constrained environment.

sessions.title: Loading the Model and Preprocessor
sessions.description: Use standard libraries to load model checkpoints and replace pretrained heads with dedicated task classifiers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back. In this session, we transition from selecting our base model to actually loading it into our programming environment, where we will perform some delicate neural surgery. The primary objective is to help learners understand what happens under the hood when we adapt a general-purpose model for a specific classification task. We want to demystify the process of loading a pretrained architecture, specifically focusing on the moment we slice off its default language modeling 'head' and graft on a brand-new, untrained classification head. For public-audience learners who appreciate a concept-first delivery, this session serves as a critical bridge showing how theoretical transfer learning translates into code-level structural changes.

To begin this lecture, draw a clear distinction on the board between the 'backbone' or 'body' of the model and its 'head'. Visualize the pretrained model as a deep feature extractor—a stack of transformer layers that has learned the syntax, grammar, and general semantic structures of language. Explain that this body remains intact. Above this, draw the original 'head', which for a masked language model is a layer designed to predict missing words from a vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens. For our classification task, this massive vocabulary predictor is useless. We must discard it and replace it with a dense layer that outputs exactly $N$ numbers, where $N$ represents our target categories, such as customer support departments. Emphasize that this structural modification is why we get warnings during initialization: we are actively discarding old knowledge at the final layer and introducing raw, uninitialized parameters.

Now, walk through the logic of initializing this architecture using standard Hugging Face AutoClasses. Explain to the learners that when they invoke `AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained()`, the library does two things simultaneously: it downloads and loads the pretrained weights for the transformer backbone, and then it automatically initializes a new classification head with random weights. Point out a common point of confusion here: many beginners freak out when they see a warning message in their console stating that some weights were not used and some weights were newly initialized. Explicitly instruct teachers to frame this warning not as an error, but as a confirmation of success. The warning is simply telling us that the language model head weights were thrown away, and the new classification head is currently full of random noise that needs to be trained.

Next, introduce an interactive mental sandbox to test this understanding. Ask the learners: 'If we run an input sentence through our newly loaded model right now, before any training, what kind of outputs should we expect?' Use this question to reveal how the random initialization of the classification head affects the model's logits. Because the classification head's weights are completely random, the initial outputs will be chaotic and untrained, representing a uniform baseline or random guesses. This sets up the perfect transition for our next session, where we will observe and document these raw baseline predictions in action.

tasks: Explain what happens when a pretrained language modeling head is replaced with a classification head.
Identify which weights are initialized randomly upon loading the classification head.

sessions.title: Running Baseline Predictions
sessions.description: Obtain output predictions from the raw initialized model before training to establish a baseline behavior.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a critical habit in machine learning: establishing a baseline prediction. The primary goal is to show learners how their newly modified model—which now has a randomly initialized classification head attached to a robust, pretrained body—behaves before a single gradient step is taken. It is essential to explain that this raw state is our yardstick. Without seeing how poorly or randomly the untrained model performs, we cannot truly quantify the progress made during fine-tuning. By setting this reference point, we demystify the 'black box' of neural network weights and build an intuitive appreciation for the training process.

To visualize this on our conceptual whiteboard, we draw a pipeline with three distinct stages. First, we feed a sample text, such as 'I love this product!', into the model. Second, we trace this text as it gets converted into input IDs and flows through the frozen, highly capable pretrained layers. Third, we focus heavily on the final classification layer. On the whiteboard, we represent this layer as a set of weights ($W$) and biases ($b$) initialized with small random numbers. We draw the mathematical transformation $y = Wx + b$, emphasizing that because these parameters are randomized, the output logits will also be arbitrary values. This random nature means the model has no contextual understanding of our specific target classes yet.

Next, the teacher should guide learners through predicting probability distributions using the softmax function. We show how the raw, arbitrary logits are scaled into a probability distribution that sums to one. A key pedagogical moment here is to address a common misconception: some learners expect a pre-trained model to already possess basic classification intelligence out-of-the-box for their custom classes. By printing the raw probabilities (e.g., 51% for Class A and 49% for Class B, or random swings), we visually prove that the model is essentially guessing. We contrast this 'untrained confidence' with a truly trained state to show that an untrained model's predictions are statistically equivalent to a coin toss, or $1/N$ where $N$ is the number of target classes.

Finally, we engage the learners in a quick mental exercise to solidify this intuition. We present them with a hypothetical three-class scenario and ask them to predict what the initial loss and classification outputs should look like. If the model starts predicting one class with 99% confidence before training, we explain that this indicates a bug or an unintended bias in weight initialization rather than natural baseline behavior. We conclude the session by saving these raw baseline predictions, setting the stage for the next phase where we will run the actual training loop and watch these random distributions transform into sharp, accurate classifications.

tasks: Observe model predictions prior to training.
Confirm that initial predictions correspond to random class weights.

lectures.title: Configuring the Training Process
lectures.description: Fine-tune hyperparameters to control the optimization loop.

sessions.title: Selecting the Training Objective
sessions.description: Define the mathematical loss objective (e.g., Cross-Entropy Loss) used to calculate errors for multi-class classification.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a foundational question that every practitioner must answer before starting fine-tuning: 'How do we mathematically measure how wrong our model is?' In a concept-first public lecture style, we will introduce the concept of the Training Objective. Instead of diving straight into calculus, we will use a visual analogy of a hot-and-cold tracking system. The loss function is that system—a single numerical gauge that tells the model whether its current predictions are getting warmer (closer to the truth) or colder (further away). By establishing this high-level intuition first, we demystify why choosing the correct objective function dictates the entire trajectory of the neural network's adaptation process.

Next, we transition to our visual whiteboard to compare two distinct classification paradigms: single-label versus multi-label classification. This is a common point of confusion for beginners who often confuse the mechanics of softmax with sigmoid. On the left side of the whiteboard, we draw a 'Single-Label' system, such as categorizing a customer feedback email as *only* 'Billing', *only* 'Technical Support', or *only* 'Refund Request'. Here, the categories are mutually exclusive. We explain how the Softmax activation converts raw model outputs (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to exactly 1, and how Cross-Entropy Loss then measures the distance between this distribution and a 'one-hot' encoded target vector. On the right side, we contrast this with a 'Multi-Label' system where a single feedback email can simultaneously be tagged as both 'Billing' and 'Technical Support'. In this scenario, we use independent Sigmoid activations for each category and apply Binary Cross-Entropy Loss across each label separately. The critical takeaway here is that choosing the wrong loss function forces the model to learn incorrect constraints, such as competing to suppress valid labels in a multi-label context.

Now, we connect the calculated loss value to the mechanism that actually updates the model's weights: backpropagation. We draw a simple feedback loop on the whiteboard. The raw inputs flow forward through the network layers to produce a prediction, the loss function evaluates the error against the ground truth, and then—crucially—this error signal is sent backward through the network. We describe this backward pass as a cascade of micro-adjustments. Using a visual metaphor of a complex sound mixing board with thousands of dials, we explain how the gradients act as instructions telling each dial whether to turn slightly left or right to decrease the overall noise (loss). We explicitly address a common developer pitfall: treating loss as a vanity metric. Beginners often assume a decreasing loss always means a better model, without realizing that if the loss objective is misaligned with the real-world goal, the model will simply become highly confident in making useless predictions.

To consolidate these concepts, we introduce an interactive whiteboard exercise. We present a mock scenario where a model is training on customer sentiment. We show a prediction distribution that assigns 80% confidence to 'Positive' when the actual tag is 'Negative'. We ask the audience to trace how this high error translates into a steep gradient signal, and conversely, how a nearly correct prediction yields a flat gradient that leaves the weights virtually unchanged. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners understand the dynamic relationship between prediction error, loss value magnitude, and the scale of the resulting parameter updates. We wrap up by highlighting that the training objective is the compass of the optimization process; if the compass points the wrong way, no amount of advanced hyperparameter tuning can save the model.

tasks: State the difference between single-label and multi-label classification loss objectives.
Explain how loss feedback drives backpropagation gradients.

sessions.title: Setting the Learning Rate
sessions.description: Analyze how step-size controls parameters updates, and the risks of choosing learning rates that are too large or too small.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing a physical intuition of the optimization process. The teacher should draw a rugged, uneven valley on the board, representing our loss landscape, with a small ball representing our current model parameters. Introduce the learning rate not merely as a numerical scalar, but as the 'stride length' of our optimizer. Explain that each step of gradient descent calculates the steepest direction downhill, but the learning rate determines exactly how far we jump in that direction. This visualization immediately anchors the mathematical formula, helping students visualize the spatial impact of their hyperparameter choices.

Now, the teacher should draw what happens when we select an excessively large learning rate. Illustrate the ball overshooting the bottom of the valley, landing high up on the opposite slope, and then ricocheting even further upward with the next step, eventually flying out of the frame entirely. Explain that this represents training divergence, where the loss values explode into infinity or NaN values. Conversely, draw a tiny learning rate where the ball moves in imperceptible, microscopic increments. Explain that while this might eventually reach the bottom, it risks getting trapped in shallow local minima, or exhausting our computational budget before making meaningful progress. The central goal here is to help learners identify the delicate sweet spot where the steps are large enough to escape minor irregularities but small enough to settle smoothly at the global minimum.

To bridge this intuition to advanced modern architectures, we transition to the concept of learning rate scheduling, specifically focusing on the warm-up phase. The teacher should plot a 2D graph with the horizontal axis representing training steps and the vertical axis representing the active learning rate. Draw a steep upward ramp at the very beginning of training. Explain that at the start of fine-tuning, the pretrained model's weights are already highly structured, but the classification head is randomly initialized. If we immediately apply a large learning rate, the massive gradients coming from the chaotic, untrained head will backpropagate into the backbone and violently corrupt the fragile, pre-existing feature detectors—a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting.

To prevent this, the teacher should illustrate how the warm-up schedule starts the learning rate at zero and scales it up linearly over the first few hundred steps. This allows the newly added parameters to adapt roughly to the data without damaging the pretrained weights. Once this initial warm-up period is complete, draw a gradual decay curve (such as cosine decay) showing how the rate steadily decreases as training progresses. This downward slope ensures that as the model approaches optimal parameter space, its step sizes shrink, preventing it from overshooting the final, delicate minimum.

Conclude the session with a formative whiteboard challenge designed to test the students' mechanical understanding of these concepts. Have them sketch the theoretical loss curve over time for two scenarios: one with a high learning rate and no warm-up, and another with a well-configured warm-up and decay schedule. Address the common student misconception that a higher learning rate always speeds up training time; point out that it often leads to instability that requires restarting training entirely. This conceptual exercise ensures they can recognize the signatures of bad learning rate configurations purely by looking at diagnostic loss plots.

tasks: Describe the physical effect of a massive learning rate on the loss landscape.
Design a standard warm-up schedule for learning rates during training.

sessions.title: Setting the Batch Size
sessions.description: Balance GPU memory consumption and training stability by selecting appropriate local batch sizes and gradient accumulation steps.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by addressing a central tension in deep learning: the struggle between mathematical stability and hardware constraints. To set the stage, draw a simple split-screen diagram on the board. On the left side, sketch 'Large Batch Size,' illustrating how processing more training samples simultaneously leads to smoother gradient vectors and stable convergence, but at the cost of massive GPU memory demand. On the right, draw 'Small Batch Size,' showing erratic, zig-zagging gradient vectors that fit comfortably in memory but introduce noise into the optimization path. The goal is to make the learner appreciate that batch size is not just an arbitrary hyperparameter, but a crucial lever balancing training quality against the hard ceiling of physical hardware.

Next, introduce the dreaded Out-of-Memory (OOM) error, a common rite of passage for anyone fine-tuning their first model. Visually map out how PyTorch allocates VRAM during a forward and backward pass, highlighting that memory is consumed not just by the model weights, but also by activation states, gradients, and optimizer states. To make this concrete, work through a real-world sizing scenario on the whiteboard: show how a batch size of 32 might crash a standard 16GB GPU, and why simply dropping the batch size to 2 resolves the crash but breaks the stability of our gradient updates. This transition naturally sets up the need for a mechanism to decouple our mathematical batch size from our hardware-constrained processing limits.

Now, introduce the concept of Gradient Accumulation as the ultimate bridge between hardware limitations and training stability. On the whiteboard, draw a horizontal timeline divided into multiple micro-batches. Illustrate step-by-step how the model processes a micro-batch of size 4, calculates the gradients, but critically, does not update the weights or clear the gradients yet. Show them accumulating over three more iterations, summing up to a virtual batch size of 16, at which point the optimizer finally executes a single weight update and clears the accumulator. Write out the simple relationship on the board: 'Effective Batch Size = Local Batch Size x Gradient Accumulation Steps.' This visual mathematical decomposition helps learners see exactly how they can simulate a high-stability training run on modest consumer hardware.

To solidify this understanding, transition to an interactive calculation exercise. Present a scenario where the student has access to an 8GB GPU. They need an effective batch size of 64 to ensure smooth convergence for their feedback classification model, but a local batch size greater than 8 triggers an immediate OOM error. Guide them to calculate the correct number of gradient accumulation steps (8). This exercise is designed to reveal whether students truly understand the multiplication relationship, preventing the common mistake of scaling learning rates proportionally without accounting for the accumulation buffer. Conclude the session by writing down a simple programmatic pseudocode snippet on the board, demonstrating where the accumulation loop hooks into the loss scaling and optimizer step calls, preparing them for practical configuration in the next session.

tasks: Calculate memory savings when using gradient accumulation to simulate large batch sizes.
Resolve common out-of-memory errors by adjusting processing batches.

sessions.title: Setting the Number of Epochs
sessions.description: Determine how many full training runs over the dataset are required to optimize performance without over-training.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by visually defining what an 'epoch' actually represents on our conceptual whiteboard. Many beginners conflate an 'epoch' with an 'iteration' or a 'step'. To resolve this immediately, draw a large circle representing the entire training dataset (e.g., 10,000 feedback comments). Then, show how this circle is divided into smaller chunks (batches). One epoch is completed only when the model has looked at every single chunk exactly once. Explain to the audience that setting the number of epochs is essentially deciding how many times the model gets to read the entire library of our training data to learn its patterns. If we set it too low, the model barely skims the pages (underfitting); if we set it too high, the model memorizes the exact punctuation and noise of our dataset (overfitting), losing its ability to generalize to new, unseen customer reviews.

Next, transition to a practical whiteboard calculation to build operational intuition. Walk the class through a simple mathematical breakdown. If our dataset has 1,000 samples and our batch size is 50, then one epoch consists of exactly 20 iterations (or steps). If we plan to run for 5 epochs, the total training loop will run for 100 steps. This calculation is crucial because training duration and GPU costs scale linearly with this number. Have the teachers guide the students to estimate their training runtime by multiplying the time taken for a single step by the total calculated steps. Introduce a common pitfall here: developers often arbitrarily set massive epoch numbers (like 50 or 100) on large transformer models, assuming 'more is better,' which leads to massive cloud compute bills and a degraded, overfitted model that fails in production.

Now, introduce the core concept of dynamic monitoring to prevent over-training: tracking the validation loss curve alongside the training loss curve. On the whiteboard, plot 'Loss' on the Y-axis and 'Epochs' on the X-axis. Draw a steadily declining line for training loss. Then, draw a second line for validation loss that initially decreases, flattens out, and then begins to curve upward. Explain that the exact point where the validation loss begins to rise—even as training loss continues to fall—is the inflection point of overfitting. This visual naturally introduces 'Early Stopping' as an automated referee. Instead of guessing the perfect number of epochs beforehand, we monitor this validation metric at the end of each epoch and halt training if it fails to improve for a set number of evaluations (the 'patience' parameter).

Conclude the session with a brief interactive thought exercise. Present the students with a hypothetical scenario: 'After epoch 3, training loss is 0.1 and validation loss is 0.4. At epoch 4, training loss drops to 0.05, but validation loss climbs to 0.6. What should you do?' This exercise forces them to apply the visual loss curve analysis to real numbers, realizing that training should have stopped at epoch 3 and that the epoch 4 model is actually worse for deployment. This sets up the perfect transition to configuring checkpoints and saving only the best-performing weights.

tasks: Estimate training time and iteration loops based on dataset size, batch size, and epoch targets.
Define indicators for stopping early during epoch tracking.

sessions.title: Configuring Checkpoints and Reproducibility
sessions.description: Implement checkpoint saving and fix random seeds to ensure consistent, verifiable experimental outcomes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a silent but devastating pain point in machine learning: the 'unreproducible run' and the catastrophic loss of hours of training due to unexpected hardware or connection drops. Given the learner's preference for a concept-first, public-lecture style, we want to frame this not as a dry exercise in software engineering, but as the foundational safety net and empirical scientific standard for any model training. The concept of determinism in neural networks must be introduced first. Explain that computers generate 'pseudo-random' numbers using a starting value called a seed. If this seed is not explicitly set, every framework—PyTorch, NumPy, Python's native random library, and even the GPU's underlying CUDA operations—will initialize randomly, resulting in slightly different weights, different data shuffles, and completely different final models, making debugging impossible.

To make this concrete, visualize a split whiteboard path. On the left side, we have 'The Chaos Pipeline' where random data shuffling, random weight initialization, and unseeded dropout layers produce a loss curve that cannot be replicated. On the right side, we draw 'The Controlled Pipeline' where a single, unified seed is broadcast to all library components. Detail how the teacher should explain the mechanism of locking down these seeds. We must walk through the systematic seeding of `random.seed()`, `np.random.seed()`, `torch.manual_seed()`, and crucially, the CUDA-specific flags like `torch.cuda.manual_seed_all()`. Explain that without securing all of these channels, a leak in randomness can still occur, particularly when multi-threaded data loaders spin up. The core takeaway here is that scientific integrity in AI relies on eliminating stochastic noise so we can isolate the actual impact of hyperparameter changes.

Next, transition to the physical reality of training: model checkpoints. A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of the model's entire state—its weights, optimizer states, learning rate scheduler configurations, and current epoch/step counter. Introduce the concept of step-wise directories. Instead of waiting for a 10-hour training run to finish and risk a system crash at hour 9, we configure the trainer to save state at regular intervals, such as every 500 steps. Explain the trade-off between disk space and recovery granularity. If we save too frequently, we fill up storage; if we save too rarely, we risk losing progress. Show how to configure a rolling checkpoint system that only keeps the best or most recent 'N' checkpoints, automatically pruning older, redundant directories.

We will now integrate an interactive troubleshooting exercise designed to address a common pitfall. The teacher should pose a scenario: 'You paused training at step 1000, loaded the saved checkpoint weights, and restarted training, but your validation loss suddenly spiked or behaved erratically compared to a continuous run. Why?' The goal of this exercise is to guide learners to realize that a true checkpoint is not just a saved model weight file (like a PyTorch `.bin` or `.safetensors` file), but must also contain the exact state of the optimizer (like Adam's momentum buffers). If you only load the weights but start with a fresh optimizer state, the optimizer has to 're-learn' the gradients from scratch, causing unstable updates. This distinction highlights why a comprehensive directory structure is necessary over a simple weight-export command.

Finally, summarize how reproducibility and checkpointing work hand-in-hand to build a robust machine learning workflow. By cementing these practices early, the learner transitions from treating AI training like a chaotic, unpredictable craft to treating it as a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline. Wrap up by outlining the structured layout of a standard output directory containing configuration files, training state JSONs, and epoch-based subfolders, preparing them to confidently initiate their first training run in the upcoming practical modules.

tasks: Configure step-wise save directories to preserve model training state.
Implement unified seeding across data loaders and model libraries.

lectures.title: Running the Fine-Tuning Job
lectures.description: Execute, track, and save the customized weights from your training environment.

sessions.title: Loading and Processing the Dataset
sessions.description: Feed your tokenized, split datasets into model training modules.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing a visual bridge from tokenization to the active training pipeline. On the left side of the whiteboard, sketch a flow representing how static tokenized text lists transition into dynamic tensors ready for GPU ingestion. Explain that while tokenization turns words into lists of integers, training requires these lists to be grouped into rectangular matrices called batches. The core objective of this session is to help learners understand that data cannot just be thrown at a model; it must be carefully structured, padded, and mapped to specific tensor keys to prevent downstream runtime errors. This sets up the conceptual necessity of PyTorch DataLoaders and Hugging Face Data Collators.

Draw a sequence of three sentences of highly variable lengths on the whiteboard to demonstrate the challenge of batching. Underneath these sentences, write out their corresponding token ID arrays. Here, introduce the concept of padding. Explain that GPUs process inputs in parallel, which mathematically requires every sequence in a single batch to have the exact same length. This is where we visually illustrate 'Dynamic Padding' versus 'Static Padding' on the board. Show how static padding to the absolute maximum model limit (like 512 tokens) wastes immense computational memory on padding tokens (represented as zeros) for short sentences. Contrast this by drawing a box around a localized batch where we pad only to the longest sequence within *that specific batch*, demonstrating a massive save in memory and computation.

Now, transition to the structural anatomy of the batch itself. Draw a diagram of the standard batch dictionary that the model expects during the training loop. On the board, write out the three critical dictionary keys: 'input_ids', 'attention_mask', and 'labels'. Walk through the logical necessity of each key. Explain that 'input_ids' hold the numerical representations of our words, 'attention_mask' tells the self-attention mechanism which tokens are real and which ones are just padding zeros to be ignored, and 'labels' guide the loss function by providing the target category IDs. Emphasize that a common point of failure for beginners is a key mismatch—such as passing 'label' instead of 'labels'—which can lead to vague, frustrating PyTorch framework errors.

To solidify this understanding, guide the instructor to introduce a conceptual verification exercise. Instruct the teacher to walk through the process of pulling exactly one test batch from the configured DataLoader before triggering the full training run. On the whiteboard, mock up the output of printing the shapes of this single batch. Show a visual representation of the tensor shape, such as [8, 34], where 8 is the batch size and 34 is the length of the longest sequence in that batch. Show how to inspect the values inside the 'attention_mask' to verify that 1s correctly represent active tokens and 0s represent padded tokens at the end of shorter sequences. This active inspection serves as a diagnostic sanity check, teaching students to catch structural issues before committing time and resources to a failing training run.

tasks: Verify that dataloaders return batches with consistent padding structures.
Inspect batched data dictionaries for correct key values.

sessions.title: Starting the Training Run
sessions.description: Initialize the training loop, feeding data to the classification model.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by drawing a high-level architectural diagram on the physical or virtual whiteboard to bridge the gap between data preparation and active model training. On the left side of the board, sketch the data loader spitting out padded batches of tokenized IDs and attention masks. In the center, draw the model itself as a multi-layered block ending with a classification head. On the right, sketch the loss calculation and the gradient feedback loop that goes back into the model weights. The primary objective of this introduction is to show students that starting a training run is not just about clicking 'run' on a script, but about initiating a complex, synchronized transfer of data between system memory and GPU hardware. Clarify that this initial transition is where most mechanical bugs, such as tensor shape mismatches, will first reveal themselves.

Transition the whiteboard lecture to focus on what happens behind the scenes when the execution command is called. Detail the sequence of events: the training configuration is validated, model parameters are copied to the target device, and the first batch of data is loaded. Explain to the students how the model's forward pass computes raw predictions (logits), how these are compared against ground truth labels to compute the cross-entropy loss, and how the backward pass computes gradients. To make this concrete, draw a timeline of the first training step on the board, marking the exact moments of data loading, forward propagation, backward propagation, and optimizer weight update. This visualization helps prevent the common misconception that training is a black-box operation, giving learners a mental model to debug performance or speed bottlenecks later.

Introduce the critical concept of hardware resource allocation, specifically focusing on Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) Video RAM (VRAM) dynamics. On the whiteboard, draw a pie chart or bar graph representing total VRAM. Partition this memory into four distinct blocks: static model weights, gradients, optimizer states (which often take up the largest share in AdamW optimization), and dynamic activation memory generated during forward passes. Explain how activation memory scales directly with batch size and sequence length. Use this breakdown to explain the dreaded Out of Memory (OOM) error, warning students that an OOM error usually occurs during the first few steps because activation memory peaks during the backward pass. Show how to monitor this resource using simple terminal utilities or library-specific telemetry, ensuring they can verify that the GPU is being actively and efficiently utilized rather than idling while the CPU does the heavy lifting.

Conclude with an interactive dry-run walkthrough where the teacher models the execution of the training process within a live workspace. Instruct the teacher to guide students to run their script and immediately pause to look at the first printed log lines. Show how to verify that the initial loss value aligns with theoretical expectations—for instance, a 3-class classification problem should start with an initial loss of approximately 1.10 (the natural logarithm of 3) if the weights are initialized randomly. This acts as a crucial sanity check. If the loss is wildly different or if the GPU memory allocation does not register a stable plateau, it indicates an issue with dataset shuffling, loss definition, or model initialization. This practice gives learners the diagnostic tools needed to confidently supervise the start of any future deep learning pipeline.

tasks: Execute the model training script in your environment.
Verify GPU active resource allocation during initial iterations.

sessions.title: Monitoring Training and Validation Loss
sessions.description: Track step logs to ensure validation loss trends downwards alongside training loss.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome learners to this crucial conceptual checkpoint on monitoring model training. In this whiteboard session, we transition from pure execution to observation and diagnosis. The core objective is to teach students how to read the 'vital signs' of a fine-tuning model using training and validation loss curves. Begin by sketching a clean set of axes on the board: the horizontal axis represents training progress (either steps or epochs), and the vertical axis represents loss. Explain that loss is our measure of error; therefore, our ultimate goal is to see these curves move downward. Introduce the two parallel tracking systems: training loss, which measures how well the model is learning from the active training data, and validation loss, which acts as an unbiased test of how well the model generalizes to unseen data.

Now, sketch the ideal scenario on the whiteboard: the curve of safe convergence. Draw a smooth, downward-sloping curve for training loss that starts high and levels out asymptotically. Right above it, draw a second curve for validation loss that mirrors this downward trend, perhaps staying slightly higher but stable. Use this visual to explain that when both curves decrease and flatten together, the model is successfully extracting generalizable patterns rather than just memorizing the training samples. Emphasize that a slight gap between training and validation loss is normal, but they should trend in harmony.

Contrast this healthy picture by drawing the two most common failure modes: overfitting and divergence. First, draw a scenario where the training loss continues to drop toward zero, but the validation loss suddenly stops decreasing and begins to curve upward. Explain this visual queue of overfitting: the model is memorizing the specific noise of the training set, losing its ability to generalize. Next, draw a chaotic, jagged curve that spikes upward or fluctuates wildly, representing divergence. Explain to the learners that this is often the calling card of an excessive learning rate, where the optimization steps are too large, causing the model to overshoot the optimal loss landscape and destabilize.

To solidify these visual concepts, transition from curves to a simulated raw log table on the whiteboard. Write down columns for 'Epoch', 'Step', 'Training Loss', and 'Validation Loss'. Walk through rows where validation loss suddenly spikes from 0.45 to 1.2 while training loss drops to 0.1, and ask learners to diagnose the issue (overfitting). Then show a table where loss values do not change at all over hundreds of steps, pointing to a frozen gradient or a learning rate set too low. This exercise bridges the gap between raw numeric outputs in a terminal and the visual intuition of model optimization, giving learners the confidence to decide whether to stop a run early or let it proceed.

tasks: Graph a model run log showing safe convergence.
Identify signs of divergence or learning rate failure from loss tables.

sessions.title: Saving the Fine-Tuned Model
sessions.description: Package parameters, vocabularies, and classification configurations into a clean output directory.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by drawing a simple, intuitive metaphor on the whiteboard: a three-compartment storage chest. The goal is to demystify what a "trained model" actually looks like when it is at rest on a hard drive. Beginners often mistake a model for a single active program, but we need to show them that it is actually a static collection of distinct files that must work in perfect harmony. On the whiteboard, label the three compartments of your drawn chest: 'The Brain' (weights), 'The Blueprint' (configuration metadata), and 'The Translator' (tokenizer). This visual anchor helps students understand that saving a model means packaging these three elements into a clean, unified directory so it can be revived anywhere without internet access.

Next, transition to a detailed breakdown of the directory structure. On the board, write out a mock directory tree representing a successfully saved model. List out files like 'model.safetensors' (or 'pytorch_model.bin'), 'config.json', and 'tokenizer_config.json'. For each file, explain its critical role. Emphasize 'config.json' as a common point of failure: explain that it contains the model's architectural dimensions and, crucially for our classification task, the mapping between numerical label IDs and human-readable text strings (such as 0 for 'Complaints' and 1 for 'Inquiries'). If this file is missing or corrupted, the raw mathematical outputs of the model cannot be translated back into meaningful predictions.

Address a major pitfall that many novice developers face: the 'vocabulary drift' and 'missing configuration' traps. Teachers should explain that saving only the model weights while forgetting to save the accompanying tokenizer will cause downstream deployment pipelines to crash or, worse, silently corrupt predictions because the model will use a different default vocabulary to tokenize input text. To prevent this, demonstrate on the board how the save function must write out both the model state and the tokenizer state to the exact same folder path. Highlight that verifying this complete payload is the first line of defense before shipping a model to production.

Conclude the session with an interactive verification walkthrough. Sketch a flowchart showing an 'Offline Test Env' that has absolutely zero internet connection. Show the process of loading the saved model locally from the output directory rather than downloading it from an online model hub. Instruct the teacher to guide students through verifying the directory contents: check for the configuration metadata file and then execute a quick reload script. This practice task reveals whether the model can successfully stand up on its own, ensuring students walk away with a fully portable, documented artifact ready for the final deployment unit.

tasks: Confirm that saved weight directories contain complete configuration metadata files.
Demonstrate reloading the saved custom model checkpoint for offline usage.

projects.stage_description: Load a pretrained DistilBERT model, configure hyperparameter training arguments (learning rate, batch size, epoch checkpoints), execute the Hugging Face Trainer run, and save the final fine-tuned model checkpoint.
projects.deliverable_increment: A saved PyTorch model checkpoint directory with config.json and pytorch_model.bin along with training logs recording validation loss decay.
