units.title: Using the Fine-Tuned Model
units.description: Package, run, and maintain your fine-tuned model safely. Learn to construct prediction pipelines, design lightweight user interfaces, analyze computational costs, and establish responsible deployment practices.

lectures.title: Creating a Usable Model
lectures.description: Transition your trained model from an experimental script to an active, testable classification service.

sessions.title: Creating an Inference Pipeline
sessions.description: Construct an inference pipeline that handles raw text inputs, tokenizes them, runs the model forward pass, and outputs human-readable labels.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by laying out the conceptual blueprint of an end-to-end inference pipeline on our visual whiteboard. For complete beginners, it is critical to address the 'black box' misconception of model deployment. Many think they can simply feed raw text into a neural network and get a clean label out. To dispel this, we construct a sequential flow chart showing raw, unstructured text entering a tokenizer, transforming into structured tensor inputs (attention masks and input IDs), passing through the neural network's forward pass to generate raw logits, and finally passing through a softmax operation paired with a label mapping lookup to output a human-readable category (like 'Complaints' or 'Inquiries'). By mapping this pipeline visually, students understand why encapsulation is necessary for building any production-level software.

Next, the whiteboard presentation shifts to the structural design of a custom pipeline class. Rather than relying on high-level prebuilt libraries that obscure the internal mechanics, we walk through the architecture of a custom Python class. We illustrate how the class initializes by loading both the tokenizer and the model from a saved directory. Students will see how the tokenizer's specific vocabulary and configuration must perfectly match the weights loaded into the classification model, or else the output will be garbage. We explicitly highlight the trap of mismatched tokenization schemes, a common pitfall where a model fails at prediction simply because a different tokenizer was used during inference than during training.

We then diagram the mechanics of the forward pass within this pipeline class. Here, the whiteboard depicts the transition from tokenized inputs to PyTorch tensors, with a strong focus on memory management and device placement (CPU versus GPU). We teach how to run the forward pass under a 'no-gradient' context manager (`torch.no_grad()`). Explaining the intuition here is crucial: omitting gradient calculations during inference dramatically reduces memory usage and speeds up computations. We visually show how keeping gradients enabled would keep an unnecessary computation graph in memory, slowing the pipeline down and risking out-of-memory errors.

Finally, we map out the post-processing layer where logits are transformed into deterministic classification labels. On the whiteboard, we show raw logits as arbitrary positive and negative floating-point numbers. We trace their path through a Softmax function, converting them into normalized probabilities that sum to one. Then, we demonstrate using an Argmax operation to isolate the index of the highest probability, which we translate into a human-readable string using a JSON label mapping dictionary stored alongside our model artifact. We wrap up by prompting the student with an exercise: given a raw prediction array, they must trace it manually to a labeled JSON schema. This confirms their understanding of label alignment before they transition to building interactive user interfaces.

tasks: Write a clean pipeline class that encapsulates tokenizer loading, forward pass execution, and post-processing.
Confirm that raw predictions match expected JSON label mappings.

sessions.title: Building a Simple Prediction Interface
sessions.description: Create a lightweight user interface (e.g., using Gradio or Streamlit) to test and showcase your fine-tuned model interactively.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the transition from a terminal-based inference pipeline to a living, interactive application. For most stakeholders and non-technical team members, a raw Python dictionary or JSON output is abstract and unconvincing. This session introduces the conceptual architecture of a model interface, mapping how a user-facing text input block binds directly to our background inference function, executing the forward pass and rendering the output in real-time. By framing the UI as a 'window' into the neural network, we help students realize that usability is the bridge between model development and real-world adoption. To visualize this, the instructor should sketch a three-part block diagram on the whiteboard: the input layer (user text), the processing engine (our fine-tuned model wrapped in its pipeline), and the output visualization (the category label accompanied by confidence scores).

Next, we dive into building the interface using a lightweight framework like Gradio. The instructor will guide the students through writing a clean Python script that imports their pipeline and wraps it within a simple UI block. The core logic chain here is functional binding: explaining how a single click trigger captures the contents of a text area, runs it through the model's tokenizer and classification head, and updates the DOM dynamically. The teacher must highlight why local state management is critical when building these interfaces—ensuring that each keystroke or query is handled isolatedly without model reload overhead. We emphasize writing a helper function that intercepts raw text inputs and maps prediction indices to friendly, high-contrast visual elements, such as probability bars, which give users immediate insight into model certainty.

A significant portion of this session is dedicated to defensive engineering—preparing the interface for the chaotic nature of real-world inputs. A common pitfall for beginners is assuming users will only input clean, well-formatted paragraphs. The instructor will walk through what happens when an empty string, accidental double-spaces, or non-ASCII characters (like emojis or foreign scripts) are submitted. Without guardrails, empty inputs can trigger tokenizer errors or shape mismatches in the model's forward pass. We introduce validation layers within our UI script: checking for zero-length strings prior to pipeline execution and returning a graceful 'Please enter valid text' warning rather than throwing a system-crashing exception. By demonstrating these edge cases live, we teach students that model robustness extends beyond training metrics into the runtime environment itself.

To consolidate learning, the session wraps up with an active testing challenge. Students are prompted to launch their local server and intentionally try to break their application using nested special characters and copy-pasted document fragments. This exercise is designed to reveal hidden assumptions about text encoding and input lengths. The instructor will conclude by showing how to interpret user interaction logs in real-time, preparing the students to observe how their fine-tuned classification model behaves under diverse, unpredictable testing scenarios.

tasks: Write a script that creates a text input box and returns model predictions visually.
Verify that the interface handles empty inputs or special characters gracefully.

sessions.title: Measuring Speed and Cost
sessions.description: Measure inference latency, compute requirements, and hosting costs to assess real-world feasibility.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a critical but frequently overlooked phase of the AI lifecycle: transitioning a model from a functional notebook prototype to an economically and operationally viable production service. The core pedagogical goal is to shift the student's mindset from raw accuracy to practical constraints, specifically balancing latency (speed) against compute budgets (cost). To establish immediate intuition, we will draw a simple quadrant on the whiteboard. The vertical axis represents 'Response Time' (from instantaneous to slow) and the horizontal axis represents 'Operational Cost' (from cheap to highly expensive). By plotting different hosting options, from serverless CPU instances to high-end dedicated GPUs, we visually demonstrate the fundamental engineering trade-offs. The instructor should emphasize that a highly accurate model is useless if it takes five seconds to categorize a single customer support ticket or costs more to run than the value of the customer's subscription.

Next, we transition into the technical methodology of measuring latency. Here, we address a common pitfall: measuring a single model inference run and assuming it represents average performance. The instructor should introduce the concept of 'warm-up runs' and statistical variance. We will explain on the whiteboard how the first inference is often slow due to initial memory allocation, cache misses, and CUDA initialization. To counter this, we introduce the practice of running a benchmark loop—specifically, executing 100 consecutive model inferences. We will visually map out how to discard the first few 'warm-up' outliers, log the execution times of the subsequent runs, and calculate the average, 95th percentile (p95), and 99th percentile (p99) latency. This statistical approach helps students anticipate real-world spikes in response times under sustained traffic.

Following latency, we dive deep into the math behind hosting costs and compute requirements. Many beginners struggle to estimate API or virtual machine costs because cloud billing models can feel abstract. To make this tangible, the instructor will write out a clear, step-by-step cost equation on the whiteboard. We will assume a scenario where the model receives a specific volume of queries per month (e.g., 100,000 customer feedback submissions). We then break down how to convert this volume into active compute hours based on our measured average latency, map those hours to specific hardware rates (such as a shared CPU instance vs. a dedicated GPU instance), and project the monthly hosting bill. This exercise directly highlights the economic benefits of model optimization techniques like quantization or distillation, showing students how making a model faster directly translates to saving real money.

Finally, we engage the students in an active reflection and calculation exercise. The instructor presents a hypothetical business scenario: a company needs to classify 500,000 incoming user messages per day. The maximum allowed response time is 200 milliseconds, and the budget is capped at fifty dollars a day. Students will use the formulas written on the board to evaluate whether our current fine-tuned model, running on their measured hardware, can meet both the speed constraint and the budget limit. This exercise is designed to reveal any lingering misunderstandings about unit conversions (e.g., milliseconds to total compute hours) and forces students to make an engineering decision: would they recommend upgrading the hardware, optimizing the model further, or adjusting the business requirements?

tasks: Calculate the average latency of 100 consecutive model inferences.
Estimate monthly API costs for hosting the model based on expected query volumes.

sessions.title: Versioning the Model
sessions.description: Implement model registry and versioning standards (e.g., Git tags, Hugging Face Hub tags) to manage model assets reliably.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To transition a fine-tuned model into a professional production environment, we must address the critical challenge of reproducibility and tracking. In this lecture, we introduce the concept of model versioning as the foundation of reliable ML systems. For a general audience, we must explain that unlike standard software where code is the only variable, machine learning introduces data and weights as dynamic components. If a model behaves unexpectedly, we cannot simply rely on the codebase version; we must pinpoint the exact checkpoint, hyperparameter configuration, and dataset iteration that produced that behavior. This visual 'whiteboard' lecture serves to connect these three pillars—code, data, and model parameters—into a unified versioning schema.

On the whiteboard, the instructor should draw three parallel lines representing the evolutionary timelines of code, data, and models. Highlight how a change in the training dataset (e.g., adding 500 newly categorized user reviews) or a tweak in the training arguments (e.g., modifying the learning rate) results in a completely new set of weight files. Draw attention to the hazard of naming files 'model_final.pt' or 'model_v2_new_fixed.pt'—a common trap that leads to massive cognitive overhead and catastrophic rollbacks. To ground this, present a scenario where a newly deployed model begins producing biased predictions; without strict versioning, rollbacks are slow, manual, and prone to breaking downstream inference pipelines.

Next, introduce the Semantic Versioning (SemVer) framework adapted specifically for machine learning models. On the board, write out the classic 'vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH' structure, but redefine what these increments mean in an ML context. Explain that a 'MAJOR' version change corresponds to a breaking change in the model's architecture or output interface (such as changing the number of target classes or replacing the backbone tokenizer), which requires changes to the downstream ingestion code. A 'MINOR' version change represents a retrained model on new data or better hyperparameters with the same architecture, improving performance without breaking the pipeline. A 'PATCH' version represents minor bug fixes in metadata, updated documentation, or a safe security patch within the wrapping code. By establishing this clear vocabulary, developers and operations teams can instantly align on the risk profile of any deployment.

We then transition to practical implementation strategies using modern tooling, specifically Git tags and Hugging Face Hub tags. The instructor should visually map out how a repository tag (e.g., 'v1.1.0') ties a specific state of the code to a specific commit of model weights. Address a common misunderstanding: model weights themselves should not be directly committed to standard Git repositories due to their size. Instead, use a model registry like Hugging Face Hub, where commits are tracked via Git LFS (Large File Storage). Show how creating a release release on the hub acts as an immutable checkpoint that your inference API can confidently pin to. If an update fails, reversing the change is as simple as pointing the inference pipeline's loading function back to the previous tag.

To cement these concepts, guide the class through an interactive exercise where they draft a deployment rollback plan. The scenario asks them to evaluate a system update where the classification model's validation accuracy improved, but its real-world latency doubled. Ask the learners to determine whether this change qualifies as a Major, Minor, or Patch release, and have them outline the steps to revert to the previous version in production if the latency proves unacceptable. Through this exercise, learners realize that semantic tagging is not just bureaucratic overhead but an active safeguard that prevents downtime and ensures consistent user experiences.

tasks: Draft a semantic versioning schema for model updates (e.g., v1.0.0 to v1.1.0).
Explain how versioning helps ensure reproducibility and safe system rollback.

lectures.title: Responsible Release and Maintenance
lectures.description: Implement ethical guidelines, licensing compliance, model documentation, and long-term monitoring systems.

sessions.title: Reviewing Bias and Privacy Risks
sessions.description: Perform a final risk review to prevent personal data exposure or systemic bias prior to release.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing the transition from model training to public or production deployment. Explain that fine-tuning is not merely a mathematical exercise in reducing loss, but an act of transferring human values and potential liabilities into a software system. On the whiteboard, draw a large circle representing the base model's knowledge space, and a smaller, highly concentrated circle representing the custom fine-tuning dataset. Highlight how this concentrated injection of domain-specific data changes the model's behavior, sometimes magnifying hidden systemic biases or exposing sensitive personal identifiable information (PII) that was buried in the fine-tuning set. 

Transition to the whiteboard visualization of 'Over-memorization versus Generalization.' Draw a spectrum with 'Pattern Extraction' on the left and 'Rote Memorization' on the right. Explain that during fine-tuning, models can suffer from catastrophic memorization, where they accidentally encode specific rows of training data—such as phone numbers, client names, or unique transaction IDs—rather than general linguistic patterns. To illustrate this, sketch an attacker querying the model with a partial prompt: 'The user with email john.doe@... is experiencing issues with...'. Show how the model completion might reconstruct the private rest of the database row. Explain to the teacher that they must emphasize this risk even if the developer believes they cleaned the data, as patterns can be reconstructed through semantic similarities.

Next, address the mechanics of Systemic Bias. On the whiteboard, map a vector space with sentiment dimensions from highly positive to highly negative. Visualize how a skewed fine-tuning dataset (for instance, one where customer feedback from a specific geographic region is consistently labeled with high frustration due to a localized shipping issue) can warp the model's underlying geometry. Show how the model mistakenly associates that entire geographic region with negative sentiment globally. Warn the students about the danger of 'feedback loops,' where a biased classifier route tickets in an unequal manner, generating more negative data from that demographic, thus worsening the bias in subsequent fine-tuning cycles.

Introduce the framework of Adversarial Auditing, or 'Red Teaming.' Draw a sequence diagram on the whiteboard: Input Probe -> Model Layer -> Response Evaluator. Instruct the teacher to show how to actively probe the model using edge cases, extreme language, or jailbreak prompts designed to trick the classifier into exhibiting biased classifications or leaking raw training sentences. Address the common misconception that simple keyword filtering is sufficient protection. Illustrate how semantic variations can easily bypass superficial filters, requiring a more robust behavioral audit before release.

Conclude by guiding the students through a practice session where they simulate an adversarial audit on a mock customer support model. Show the teacher how to guide students to construct five distinct testing prompts designed to trigger biased classifications or reveal mock customer identities. Emphasize that documenting these risks in a structured release report is not about achieving a perfect zero-risk model, which is impossible, but about establishing clear risk mitigation thresholds, defining operational boundaries, and maintaining transparency with downstream stakeholders.

tasks: Audit the model with adversarial inputs to check for harmful or unexpected responses.
Document potential bias risks in your final release report.

sessions.title: Checking Dataset and Model Licenses
sessions.description: Verify compliance with both base model and dataset licenses to ensure permission for commercial or educational use.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to our journey of responsibly releasing AI models. In this whiteboard session, we will address a critical but frequently overlooked aspect of fine-tuning: compliance with licensing agreements. Many practitioners assume that if code or weights are accessible on public hubs like Hugging Face, they can be freely modified and commercialized. This is a dangerous misconception. Today, we will visually dissect the differences between datasets and base models, and map out how their respective licenses intersect. 

Let us begin our whiteboard illustration by drawing a split screen. On the left, we place our 'Base Model' (for example, a pre-trained LLM), and on the right, we place our 'Fine-Tuning Dataset'. Under each, we will write down the license terms. The first major concept to convey is that a fine-tuned model is legally and technically a derivative work. This means its release and usage are bound by the most restrictive terms of *both* the base model and the training dataset. We will draw arrows converging from both sides into a central box representing our final 'Fine-Tuned Model' to visualize how these licensing constraints merge.

Now, let us examine common base model licenses. We will write down three categories on the whiteboard: Permissive Open Source (like Apache 2.0 or MIT), Open-weights with Restrictive Clauses (such as LLaMA's community licenses, which might restrict commercial scale or specific use cases), and Research-Only licenses. A critical pitfall for developers is fine-tuning a model released under a 'non-commercial' or 'research-only' license (such as some variants of early open models) on their proprietary customer data, hoping to deploy it in a paid application. We must emphasize that even if the customer data is yours, the underlying model weights cannot be legally exploited commercially. We will draw a red 'X' through any pathway that attempts to commercialize a research-only base model.

Next, we transition to the dataset side of our whiteboard. Datasets have their own licenses, often governed by Creative Commons (CC) terms. We will write out and define 'CC-BY' (attribution required), 'CC-BY-NC' (non-commercial use only), and 'CC-0' (public domain). We will prompt the class to consider this scenario: What happens if you take a highly permissive base model (Apache 2.0) and fine-tune it on a dataset scraped from the web that is licensed under CC-BY-NC? Even though the model was free for commercial use, the resulting derivative model is now contaminated by the non-commercial restriction of the training data. We will draw a flow chart showing this 'inheritance of restrictions' to visually solidify this concept.

To round out the session, we will introduce a brief interactive sanity-check exercise. We will present a hypothetical scenario: a startup wants to build a customer feedback classifier using a base model licensed under a custom restrictive license that forbids use in 'automated customer interaction' and fine-tunes it using feedback data that has a strict internal distribution license. We will guide the class to trace where the license conflict lies. This practice teaches learners to proactively perform an audit before starting a GPU-intensive training run, saving legal and financial headaches later.

tasks: Identify potential licensing conflicts when using a research-only base model on commercial customer data.
Define the terms of standard open-source licenses like Apache 2.0 or Creative Commons.

sessions.title: Documenting Intended Use and Limitations
sessions.description: Write a clear Model Card documenting intended use cases, performance metrics, out-of-scope scenarios, and known limitations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a large, empty template of a 'Model Card' on the board. The instructor should introduce the Model Card not as bureaucratic paperwork, but as the model's official 'driver's license' and safety manual combined. For public-facing or enterprise AI, transparent documentation is the primary defense against downstream misuse and unexpected failures. The instructor will sketch out the main headers: Model Details, Intended Use, Factors, Metrics, Evaluation Data, Training Data, and Quantitative Analyses, highlighting that today we are focusing deeply on the 'Intended Use and Limitations' sections, which act as the ethical boundaries of our newly trained customer feedback classifier.

Next, the instructor will write 'INTENDED USE' on the whiteboard and map out its key components. This section must define exactly who the model is for, what tasks it is designed to perform, and what inputs it expects. The instructor should explain that for our running project—the customer feedback classifier—the intended use is categorizing English-language text feedback into predefined buckets like billing, technical support, and feature requests. To make this concrete, the instructor will draw a simple system architecture on the board showing how a clean user query flows safely into the model, and contrast this with a 'noisy' or multilingual query to illustrate how easily a model's performance can degrade if its input boundaries are not clearly defined in the documentation.

Moving to the critical counterpart, the instructor writes 'LIMITATIONS & OUT-OF-SCOPE' on the whiteboard in a distinct color, perhaps red. The primary pedagogical goal here is to dispel the misconception that admitting limitations makes a model look weak; in reality, explicit limitations protect developers from liability and prevent dangerous system failures. The instructor will sketch a 'Safe Zone' vs. 'Danger Zone' diagram. For instance, while our feedback classifier is highly accurate at routing standard customer inquiries, it is entirely unfit for critical tasks like identifying threats of self-harm or screening legal documents. The instructor will guide the class in brainstorming three specific scenarios where the model must not be deployed, emphasizing how to write these limitations clearly so that a non-technical product manager or downstream developer immediately understands the risks of misuse.

To solidify these concepts, the instructor will run an interactive drafting exercise. On the board, the instructor writes a poorly drafted limitation, such as 'The model might make mistakes sometimes,' and asks why this is useless. The instructor then refines it live into a professional statement: 'This model is trained on short customer emails and may perform poorly on long-form documents or legal contracts. It does not detect sarcasm or urgent crisis language.' This demonstrates how precise technical limitations guide real-world implementation and system guardrails.

Finally, the instructor wraps up the session by summarizing how this Model Card ties into the broader deployment pipeline. A well-documented model card ensures that when the model is handed over to software engineers or external users, they understand its functional envelope. The instructor leaves the completed Model Card visual on the board as a reference point for the upcoming sessions on feedback collection and drift detection.

tasks: Draft a comprehensive 'Intended Use' section for your customer feedback classifier.
List three scenarios where your model should not be used due to safety or accuracy concerns.

sessions.title: Collecting Feedback and Detecting Drift
sessions.description: Monitor model performance over time to detect data drift and collect user feedback for future updates.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the common misconception that once an AI model is trained and deployed, the job is complete. Introduce the whiteboard with a drawing of a static model versus a dynamic, shifting real world. Explain that unlike traditional software, machine learning systems suffer from silent degradation. This sets up the absolute necessity of active monitoring, positioning the concepts of feedback collection and drift detection not as optional add-ons, but as the essential nervous system of any production AI pipeline.

On the left side of the whiteboard, draw a clear distinction between two primary types of model degradation: Data Drift and Concept Drift. Use a customer support routing model as a concrete example to ground these definitions. Explain that Data Drift occurs when the statistical properties of the input data change—for example, if users suddenly start writing support tickets in a new slang or using different formatting, even though the underlying meaning of the categories remains the same. Contrast this with Concept Drift, where the relationship between the input and the target label itself shifts over time—such as a specific term like 'viral' transitioning from meaning a computer security threat to meaning a highly successful marketing post. Explain how both of these phenomena cause accuracy to plummet, and why they are so hard to spot because the model will still confidently output predictions without throwing any system errors.

Transition to the right side of the board to design an intuitive, user-facing feedback loop. Sketch a simple user interface showing a model prediction alongside clean, low-friction feedback mechanisms like thumbs-up/thumbs-down icons, flagging options, or quick categorization dropdowns. Explain the teacher's strategy here: emphasize that user feedback is gold, but must be collected ethically and without causing user fatigue. Warn the instructor to highlight a common pitfall: selection bias in feedback. If only highly frustrated users click the 'report error' button, your feedback dataset will be skewed. Teach the strategy of sampling a small percentage of random predictions for manual verification alongside user-flagged samples to maintain an unbiased view of actual performance.

Next, address how to detect drift programmatically when explicit human feedback is scarce. Introduce the concept of distribution monitoring. Sketch a bar chart showing the baseline distribution of predicted classes from the training phase (e.g., 20% refund requests, 50% technical issues, 30% shipping questions). Draw a second bar chart next to it showing a sudden spike in production where refund requests jump to 70%. Explain to the students that a dramatic shift in predicted class distribution is one of the easiest, most computationally inexpensive early warning indicators that either the real world has changed or the model is malfunctioning, requiring no manual labeling to detect.

Conclude the session with an interactive scenario-based exercise. Present the running customer feedback classifier project and ask the students to outline a mock telemetry log. Instruct them to identify three specific trigger events—such as a sudden surge in unclassified terms, a drop in user agreement rates, or a shift in average input length—and determine what threshold should trigger an automated alert. This hands-on visualization bridges the gap between high-level intuition and the practical steps needed to keep their models accurate over time, preparing them directly for the next session on model retraining and rollbacks.

tasks: Design a feedback mechanism for users to flag incorrect model predictions.
Define indicators that suggest input data has changed significantly since training.

sessions.title: Updating or Rolling Back the Model
sessions.description: Establish clear processes to roll back to a previous version if problems arise, and set up retraining cycles to keep your model accurate.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing a harsh reality of production AI: the day you deploy your model is not the end of the journey, but the beginning of its active maintenance. Use the whiteboard to draw a timeline of a model's lifetime, illustrating that real-world data is dynamic, and model performance will inevitably degrade due to shifting user behaviors or system bugs. Introduce the core objective of this session: establishing safety nets (rollbacks) and growth loops (retraining). Explain that a rollback strategy is your emergency brake when things go wrong instantly, while retraining is the regular tune-up that keeps the model aligned with reality over time.

On the whiteboard, sketch a simple architecture diagram representing a 'Blue-Green' deployment pattern modified for machine learning models. Draw two boxes: one labeled 'Model V1 (Stable/Active)' and another labeled 'Model V2 (New/Candidate)'. Show a router sitting in front of them, directing user traffic. Explain to learners that when deploying an updated model, we never overwrite the old model file. Instead, we keep both active. If Model V2 begins exhibiting anomalous behavior—such as unexpected classification errors or high latency—the router can instantly point 100% of the traffic back to Model V1. Emphasize that a common pitfall here is schema mismatch: if Model V2 outputs predictions in a different JSON format than Model V1, a raw rollback will crash the downstream application. The teacher should highlight the absolute necessity of keeping API contracts identical between versions.

Transition the whiteboard drawing into a circular 'Flywheel' diagram to explain the retraining lifecycle. Start with 'Production Model', pointing to 'User Feedback & Drift Alerts' (established in the previous session), which flows into 'Data Quarantine & Curation', then to 'Incremental Retraining', and finally back to 'Automated Evaluation' before redeployment. Address a critical theoretical danger here: Catastrophic Forgetting. Explain that if we retrain our customer feedback classifier *only* on the new drifted data (e.g., holiday-season complaints), it will completely forget how to classify normal, year-round feedback. To prevent this, explain the golden rule of retraining: always mix a representative baseline sample of your original training dataset with your newly collected dataset.

Engage the learners in a practical drafting exercise. Ask them to design a concrete 'Emergency Rollback Plan' checklist. Walk through the questions they must answer: What is the maximum acceptable error rate before an automated rollback is triggered? Who has the authority to click the rollback button? How do we notify the engineering team? By asking these questions, learners realize that model management is a cross-disciplinary practice combining data science, system operations, and product management.

Conclude the session by drawing a decision matrix on the board to help learners establish a sustainable retraining schedule. Contrast 'Scheduled Retraining' (e.g., every first Sunday of the month) with 'Event-Driven Retraining' (triggered automatically when data drift metrics cross a specific statistical threshold). Explain that for their first model, a hybrid approach is best: start with a manual, scheduled review to maintain human-in-the-loop oversight, and transition to automated triggers only when the pipeline's stability and evaluation metrics are thoroughly trusted.

tasks: Draft a rollback plan for restoring a stable model version if a deployment fails.
Outline a retraining schedule based on feedback and data drift indicators.
